academicTalks.transcript: Today let's talk about how coral reefs are responding to rising ocean temperatures. Coral reefs are built by tiny animals called coral polyps, which live in a close partnership with microscopic algae. These algae give coral its color and much of its energy through photosynthesis. When water gets too warm, the algae leave the coral, a process called bleaching, and the coral turns white and becomes stressed. For years, scientists assumed that most coral colonies had little ability to handle this heat. Recent studies, though, have found that some coral colonies show early signs of heat tolerance — they can survive slightly warmer water without bleaching as severely as their neighbors. Researchers believe this tolerance may come from certain algae partners that handle heat better, or from genetic differences within the coral itself. To understand the bigger picture, teams are now tracking biodiversity loss across affected reefs, comparing areas with heat-tolerant colonies to areas without them. If scientists can identify what makes these colonies more resilient, that knowledge could help guide future reef conservation efforts worldwide.

options.text: How ocean currents influence the migration patterns of coral larvae
How rising ocean temperatures are causing widespread coral bleaching worldwide

How reef ecosystems recovered completely after previous bleaching events

questions.explanationZh: 演講主軸為部分珊瑚展現「early signs of heat tolerance」，故為正解。其餘選項皆非本篇主旨。

Its polyps begin reproducing at a much faster rate
Its surface gradually darkens due to increased stress hormones

transcript.text: I missed my connecting train because my first one arrived late.

That's a relief. When does the next train leave?
In about forty minutes, from platform six. I'll print your new ticket now.
Thank you so much for sorting this out.
Of course — just make sure to board a little early this time.

academicTalks.transcript: Let's look at how a well-known regional music festival got its start. Long before it became a major event with large stages and ticketed crowds, the festival began as a simple gathering of traveling musicians who met once a year to trade songs and techniques. These musicians moved between towns, often performing in exchange for food or lodging, and their informal gatherings gradually attracted local audiences. A regional museum eventually began collecting recordings of these early performances, preserving them in an archive that still exists today. Those recordings capture styles that might otherwise have been lost, including certain playing techniques unique to this region. Over the following decades, the gathering grew into an organized festival, though organizers worked hard to keep its informal spirit alive. Today's performers often study the archived recordings directly, blending the older traveling-musician style with the festival's now-modern stages and sound systems. This connection between old and new is part of what makes the festival distinct from other regional music events, giving audiences a direct link to its earliest days.

questions.stem: What is the talk mainly about?

options.text: Two competing festivals and their rival histories in the region
A famous musician's rise to fame
How a regional festival started and was recorded
Modern ticket prices at regional festivals today

questions.explanationZh: 全篇講述音樂節如何從傳統音樂人聚會發展而來，並提及博物館保存早期錄音，故「地區音樂節如何開始並被記錄下來」為正解。原文未提及對立的音樂節，未討論票價，也不是單一音樂人的傳記，其餘選項均無根據。

questions.stem: How did the festival begin?

options.text: As a competition organized by a local government
As a fundraiser for a music school
As a broadcast event on regional radio
As an informal gathering of traveling musicians

questions.explanationZh: 原文說音樂節起源於「informal gathering of traveling musicians」，故為正解。其餘選項均未於原文中提及。

questions.stem: What did the regional museum do?

options.text: Trained new musicians to perform at festivals
Sold tickets for the earliest gatherings held annually
Preserved recordings of early performances
Organized annual concerts featuring traveling musicians across many towns

questions.explanationZh: 原文提到博物館「collecting recordings of these early performances」並建立archive保存至今，故「保存早期演出的錄音」為正解。其餘選項在原文中皆無根據，屬於干擾選項。

questions.stem: How do the archived recordings influence today's performers?

options.text: They use them only for academic research, not performance
They avoid them entirely to protect their own original style
They study them and blend old techniques with modern staging
They replaced modern instruments with historical ones entirely

questions.explanationZh: 原文提到表演者「study the archived recordings directly, blending」舊風格與現代舞台結合，故選「研究這些錄音，並把舊技法與現代舞台結合」。其餘選項皆與原文矛盾或無根據。

academicTalks.transcript: During the early industrial period, factory workers in many growing cities faced extremely long shifts, sometimes lasting fourteen hours or more without a scheduled break. Conditions in these factories were often unsafe, and injuries were common. Frustrated by these demands, groups of workers began organizing after a series of especially long shifts, forming committees to negotiate directly with factory owners. When owners refused to change their practices, workers organized public demonstrations, drawing attention from local newspapers and eventually from lawmakers. Their persistence led to a significant outcome: a new law was passed that limited the number of hours an employee could be required to work each day. This law didn't apply to every industry at first, but it set an important precedent. Over the following years, similar rules spread to other sectors as more workers organized using the same strategies. Historians consider this an early labor reform movement, one that later influenced national labor policy far beyond the cities where it began, shaping how governments regulated working hours for generations afterward.

questions.stem: What is the main focus of the talk?

options.text: An early labor reform movement
New machinery invented for factories
Wage comparisons across different industries
The founding of a single specific factory

questions.explanationZh: 全篇描述工人組織、抗爭、立法限制工時，並指出此為「early labor reform movement」且影響後世勞工政策，故（a）為正解；其餘選項皆未在原文提及。

questions.stem: Why did factory workers begin organizing?

options.text: They wanted higher pay than office workers
Shifts were too long and conditions unsafe
They opposed introducing new machinery entirely
They were protesting the factory's chosen new location

questions.explanationZh: 原文指出工人因「extremely long shifts」與「unsafe」的工作環境而開始組織委員會，故「輪班時間過長且工作環境不安全」正確；其餘選項於原文中並無根據。

questions.stem: What did the new law do?

options.text: Guaranteed workers a fixed daily wage
Limited the number of hours an employee could work each day
Required factories to provide housing for workers
Banned the use of certain factory machines

questions.explanationZh: 原文明確指出新法「limited the number of hours…each day」，故為正解。其餘選項均無根據。

questions.stem: What can be inferred about the movement's long-term impact?

options.text: It later influenced national labor policy beyond its original cities
It had no effect outside the original factories
It was quickly reversed once the law passed
It was limited entirely to one specific industry

questions.explanationZh: 原文說此運動「later influenced national labor policy far beyond the cities」，故為正解。其餘選項均與原文矛盾。

academicTalks.transcript: Let's examine how one company changed its decision-making by building a customer feedback system into its sales process. After every purchase, the company now adds a short survey asking customers to rate their experience and leave optional comments. This might seem like a small addition, but it generates a steady stream of data the company didn't have before. Each month, managers from different departments meet to review trends in the survey results, looking for patterns such as recurring complaints or repeated praise for a particular feature. These monthly reviews have become a central part of company strategy: when the feedback consistently points to a problem, that information shapes decisions about new products before they're even designed. For example, if survey comments repeatedly mention wanting a smaller version of a popular item, the product team can factor that directly into early planning. Rather than guessing what customers want, the company now bases many decisions on direct, ongoing feedback. This approach has become a model that other departments within the company are beginning to adopt for their own planning processes.

questions.stem: What is the talk mainly about?

options.text: How to train employees to handle customer complaints
How a company uses customer feedback to guide business decisions
How companies set prices for new products
How advertising influences customer purchasing habits

questions.explanationZh: 演講主軸為公司如何運用顧客回饋系統來引導決策，故為正解。其餘選項皆非本篇主旨。

questions.stem: When does the company ask customers to complete a survey?

options.text: Once a year, during a company event
After every purchase
Only when a customer files a complaint
Before a customer decides to buy anything

questions.explanationZh: 原文說「after every purchase」公司會加入問卷，故為正解。其餘選項均無根據。

questions.stem: What do managers do with the survey results each month?

options.text: Review trends and look for patterns
Send personalized replies to every customer
Delete outdated feedback automatically
Publish the results publicly online

questions.explanationZh: 原文提到經理們每月「review trends…looking for patterns」，故為正解。其餘選項均無根據。

questions.stem: How does customer feedback influence new products?

options.text: It replaces the need for a product design team
It only affects marketing slogans, not the products themselves
It is reviewed but rarely acted upon
It directly shapes early planning decisions, such as sizing

questions.explanationZh: 原文舉例回饋提到想要「smaller version」，產品團隊便納入早期規劃，故為正解。其餘選項均與原文矛盾。
